## Results

The PEEK in nanofiber membranes (PIMs), PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs), and COF-TpPa-modified PEEK nanofiber membranes (CPMs) before and after thermal compression treatment were developed (if not emphasized later, CPMs refer to CPMs-II in the Supplementary Information). The mean diameter of the PMs was approximately 0.16 ± 0.1 μm (Supplementary Figs. 3–5), and no obvious adhesion between individual nanofibers was observed. Due to the increase of the viscosity of the casting solution, the diameter of PIMs-Pa increased to 1.02 μm, which may significantly influence the characteristics of the prepared membrane (Supplementary Table 1). For the CPMs, axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF nanoarrays uniformly appeared on the surface of the nanofibers, and the diameter and length of the pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray were 45.4 and 151.6 nm, respectively (Fig. 1e, f). The diameter of the CPMs (approximately 1.44 μm) was approximately equal to the sum of the diameter of the pure PIM-Pa membrane (1.02 μm) and the thickness of the nanoarrays, indicating that the growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer greatly increased the diameter of the fibers (Fig. 1b, c and Supplementary Fig. 5). Notably, the morphology of the PMs and CPMs after thermal compression treatment was identical to that of the PMs and CPMs without thermal compression treatment (Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating that the as-prepared nanofibers could maintain shape stability even under a pressure of 5.0 MPa during the thermal treatment. In addition, the thickness of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes increased from 59.1 to 90.2 μm after the in situ growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray due to the uncompacted stacking of thicker fibers, which may also reduce the mass transfer resistance during the separation process (Supplementary Fig. 7)4. Moreover, the growth of nanoarrays greatly improves the specific surface area of the prepared membrane, expanding the steric hindrance between the oil molecules and membrane surface (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Interestingly, the in situ growth of the COF nanoarray layer regulates the crystallinity of PEEK molecules, and transmission electron microscopy confirmed the formation of interpenetrated structures between crystal regions (Fig. 1g)14,15. Before thermal compression, the PMs were amorphous, while one type of lattice fringe with the 0.22 nm d-spacing was observed for the PMs after thermal treatment (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). The lattice fringe of COF-TpPa with d-spacing of 0.3 nm appeared on the CPMs before thermal compression (Supplementary Fig. 9c)16. Notably, the introduction of COFs led to the disappearance of most of the lattice fringes of the PMs, and the electron diffraction pattern demonstrated the transformation from a single crystal to polycrystalline with a variety of lattice fringes with different d-spacings after thermal treatment (Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 9c). Furthermore, d-spacings within the crystalline domains of PEEK and COF-TpPa exhibited a marginal increase, attributable to lattice distortion arising from the thermally induced slip of COF crystals by PEEK16,17. Moreover, the surface roughness of the nanofiber membranes increased by 30%-85% after the formation of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer (Supplementary Fig. 10), which could affect the surface energy of the membrane18,19. Interestingly, the membrane aperture and membrane porosity increased by 105% and 102%, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12), because the COF-TpPa nanoarray increased the distance between the nanofibers.

According to density functional theory, the Gibbs free energy of molecules in different reaction stages was calculated to clarify the limit of the thermodynamic direction of the chemical reaction process20. The energy barrier of p-phenylenediamine bound to PEEKi is 72.3 kcal/mol, which is less than that bound to aniline. Therefore, p-phenylenediamine alleviated the hydrolysis process of PEEKi oxime (Fig. 1h)18. Interestingly, aniline, the byproduct of oxime hydrolysis, would not exert significant negative feedback on the formation process of COF-TpPa due to the large Gibbs free energy of reaction between aniline and Tp (Supplementary Fig. 13)21. On the basis of the above experimental and simulation results, the mechanism of the formation of the unique microstructure of the CPMs was speculated. As mentioned above, the hydrolysis of PEEKi and in situ growth of COF-TpPa simultaneously occurred in n-octanoic acid solutions. Since the solubility and diffusion rate of Pa in n-octanoic acid were far lower than the rate of COF-TpPa formation, especially the -CHO of Tp, which was activated to -C+HOH by n-octanoic acid in the solvent (Supplementary Fig. 14)22, the in situ growth of the COF-TpPa layer mainly occurred at the interface between the nanofibers and n-octanoic acid. With the continuous diffusion and dissolution of an appropriate content of Pa, the formation of an axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray on the top surface of PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs) was induced and inserted (Fig. 2a). Notably, as the Pa content increased, the COF-TpPa layer formed distinct nanostructures, including nanobulges, pine-needle-shaped nanoarrays, and nanoflowers (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). This morphological evolution was driven by the number of surface Pa reactive sites and the enhanced diffusion rate (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 15). After the formation of the COF-TpPa nanoarray, the hydrolysis of PEEKi became easier without the inhibition caused by Pa. Simultaneously, the hydrolysis of PEEKi released aniline, which reduced the steric hindrance of the subsequent thermal rearrangement crystallization process so that the thermal rearrangement of the polymer chain was easier to carry out (Fig. 2b).

This sequential crystallization could optimize the compatibility between COF and PEEK crystals and avoid phase separation. Therefore, the molecules of crystalline PEEK and COF-TpPa formed a hetero-interpenetration crystal structure, and the noncrystalline PEEK molecules wrapped the interpenetrating crystals to form mechanically interlocked structures23–25. The changes in the chemical structure and properties of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes further confirmed the above speculation (Supplementary Figs. 16–19 and Supplementary Table 2), which are discussed in detail in the Supplementary Infomation11,26,27. The sequential crystallization of COF-TpPa and PEEK could be confirmed by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 20). PEEKi and PEEK were fully amorphous after electron pinning, with no characteristic diffraction peaks. Notably, only the COF-TpPa crystal pattern (2θ = 4.6°) appeared in the XRD pattern of the CPMs before thermal treatment. The crystallinity of COF-TpPa was approximately 13.0%. After thermal compression treatment, new characteristic peaks belonging to the PEEK crystal region (2θ = 18.2°) in the PMs and CPMs were observed28. In addition, the XRD characteristic diffraction peaks of both COF-TpPa and PEEK shifted to the left, which also confirmed the increase in d-spacing caused by the interpenetration between the COF crystal and the PEEK crystal23,27–30. The crystallinity (41.4%) of PEEK in CPMs was slightly lower than that in PMs (43.3%) since COF-TpPa restricted the rearrangement of the molecular chain of PEEK, thereby limiting their crystallization (Supplementary Table 3)29–31. The melting temperature of PMs was approximately 250 °C, but the CPMs did not melt even at 400 °C (Supplementary Fig. 21). Moreover, the (Tg) of the CPMs increased by 15.1 °C after the introduction of the COF-TpPa layer and the sequential crystallization of the COF and PEEK (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 22)32. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations show that compared with the original PEEK, the free volume of PEEK containing COF-TpPa is reduced by 37.8%, indicating that the introduction of COF-TpPa limits the movement of the PEEK main chain and causes a decrease in crystallinity, as mentioned above (Supplementary Fig. 23). Consequently, the glass transition temperature of CPMs is higher than that of PMs. The tensile strength of the PIM was approximately 2.3 MPa (Fig. 2e). The rigid structure of PEEK contributes to its high tensile strength. Interestingly, the crystallization process of PEEK increased its tensile strength by 121.7%. The strength of the CPMs after sequential crystallization increased to 16.2 MPa, which was comparable with that of laboratory-made ultrafiltration membranes fabricated by nonsolvent-induced phase inversion (Supplementary Fig. 24). Notably, the increase in tensile strength was positively correlated with the content of the COF-TpPa (Supplementary Table 4), which showed that the introduction of a COF had a great influence on the mechanical properties of PEEK. As mentioned above, COF-TpPa is a crystalline material composed of conjugated aromatic rings, showing strong intrinsic rigidity11. Moreover, the molecular rearrangement transforms randomly because the thermal compression arranges the molecular chain segments of PEEK into long-range ordered arrangements. The hetero-interpenetration crystal structure formed by COF-TpPa and crystalline PEEK molecules contributed to the increase in the tensile strength of each nanofiber33. Interestingly, the introduction of COF led to an increase in the proportion of the amorphous region, which could absorb energy through slip and conformational changes in the molecular chain when subjected to external force, thereby increasing the elongation at break of the nanofiber membrane (Fig. 2f)34,35. The mechanical interlocking structure formed by amorphous molecules and hetero-interpenetration crystal structures optimistically increases the mechanical properties of nanofiber membranes. In addition, the nanofiber membranes were stacked by every single nanofiber of the CPMs, as mentioned above. The stacking of the axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray improved the interactive force (friction force) between different nanofibers, which could increase the mechanical strength of the prepared membrane by dispersing the force between the fibers through friction (Fig. 2f). Significantly, compared with PMs, CPMs have unparalleled stability in most organic solvents. The CPMs still maintained the shape of intact fibers after soaking in various organic solvents for 180 days, but the fibers of the PMs partially collapsed, which may have been caused by incomplete hydrolysis (Supplementary Fig. 25). Interestingly, the COF nanoarrays collapsed in some solvents, resulting in a slight decrease in tensile strength, which also proved that pine-needle-like nanoarrays between different fibers could enhance the tensile properties of the prepared membranes by dispersing external forces via friction. Notably, the prepared CPMs still had high tensile strength and elongation at break (Fig. 2g).

Interestingly, the COF-TpPa nanoarray excellently increased the surface energy of the PMs. The PMs demonstrated high hydrophobicity and underwater superoleophilicity, with a stable water contact angle of approximately 135.1° and a zero degree of underwater oil contact angle (UWOCA). However, water droplets could spread on the surface of the CPMs in less than 1.0 s, and the UWOCA of the CPM membranes was above 150.3°, indicating that the hydrophobic surface of the PM had transformed into a superhydrophilic surface after in situ radical growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Movies 1, 2 and Fig. 26). The underwater oil rolling angle of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes decreased to 5.4° after the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarrays (Supplementary Figs. 27, 28 and Supplementary Movie 3). In addition, unlike the superoleophilic PMs, the CPMs exhibited excellent oil repellency, and the adhesion force of the underwater oil droplets was less than 1.0 μN (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Movie 4 and Supplementary Fig. 29). The increase (51.8 times) in the apparent surface tension of the polar components caused by the abundant conjugated oxygen-containing groups in COF-TpPa and increased surface roughness (58.5%) on the nanofiber surface account for the reversal of surface hydrophilicity (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 30)36.

As a kind of hydrophobic material, the water adsorption capacity of PM is as low as 0.8 g g−1. After the formation of the COF-TpPa crystal nanoarray layer, the water adsorption capacity was nearly 14.8 times greater than that of the PMs since the CPMs contained many water adsorption sites and conjugated oxygen-containing groups (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 31)37. Moreover, the endothermic peak of the water-melting process shifted from 0.29 to 4.26 °C with more melting enthalpy (156.49 J/g) after the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarray. Similarly, the content of nonrefrigerated water in the CPMs (37.7%) was much greater than that in the PMs (18.4%) (Fig. 3e). In addition, the peak area ratios of intermediate water (3216 and 3400 cm−1) and free water (3544 and 3700 cm−1) increased from 0.21 to 1.75 according to Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3f; Supplementary Fig. 32 and Supplementary Table 5), which further proved that the water binding capacity of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes significantly increased as well38. According to the MD simulation, the CPM membranes exhibited stronger electrostatic interactions with water (Ecoul), which could induce a stronger binding ability with water (Fig. 3g, h)39. The water molecular diffusion coefficients in the hydration layers of the PM and CPMs were 2.6 and 2.0 m2/s, respectively. Moreover, the residence time of the CPM hydration layer was also greater than that of the PM hydration layer. The lower diffusion coefficient and greater water residence time in the CPMs could also account for their greater ability to form a hydration layer (Supplementary Fig. 33)40. In addition, the ability to form hydrogen bonds between water and the PNMs and the lifetime of the hydrogen bonds increased by 62.5% and 58.6%, respectively, after the introduction of COF-TpPa nanoarrays (Fig. 3j and Supplementary Fig. 34), which was attributed to the formation of hydrophilic COF nanoarrays on the fiber providing a large number of potential hydrogen bond acceptor sites and donor sites. (Supplementary Fig. 35)37.

The superhydrophilic surface of the engineered membrane significantly expands its potential applications in diverse operational environments, such as oil-water separation. Owing to the intrinsically hydrophobic surface, the pristine PM had a low permeance of 3.2 × 103 L m−2 h−1 bar−1, with a separation efficiency of 92.7% for water-in-octane emulsions. The permeance of the CPMs increased significantly by at least 968% and was positively correlated with the content of COF-TpPa (Fig. 4a; Supplementary Figs. 36 and 37), and the separation efficiency of the CPMs was above 99.9% (Fig. 4a). The increased permeance and separation efficiency after in situ radical growth of the COF-TpPa crystal layer could be attributed to the finely tailored membrane structures and affinities with water during the dynamic crystal engineering process, according to both the experimental and simulation results mentioned above. The COF-TpPa nanoarray layer increased the mean pore size of the nanofiber membranes, reducing the mass transfer resistance (Supplementary Fig. 38). The improvement in the affinity between the nanofiber membranes and water caused by the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer during the sequential crystallization process promoted the formation of a rigid hydration layer and encouraged water to pass through the nanofiber membranes while preventing the formation of oil droplets (Fig. 4d). More importantly, the mean particle size of the oil droplets in the filtrate of CPM was less than 100 nm, which was far smaller than that in the feed emulsion (1000 nm) and in the filtrate of PMs (500 nm) (Supplementary Fig. 38). Notably, the average pore diameter of the CPMs was greater than 3 μm, indicating that the separation of the oil-water emulsions was dependent mainly on the different Laplace repulsions caused by the different wettabilities toward water and oil2,39,40. The CPMs were also effective at disposing of various oil-in-water emulsions, such as toluene-in-water emulsions and soybean-in-water emulsions (Supplementary Figs. 39–41).

During the separation process of nanofiber membranes, the oil droplets tend to adhere and embed into the nanofiber membranes via hydrophobic interactions under transmembrane pressure due to the flexible segment and hydrophobicity of the polymer, resulting in severe irreversible membrane fouling, which limits the application of nanofiber membranes in oil/water separation (Supplementary Fig. 42). The PM exhibited severe irreversible fouling since the permeance decreased to 7.0 × 102 L m−2 h−1 bar−1, and the separation efficiency correspondingly decreased to 80% after 100 fouling-washing cycles. The interaction between the oily cake layer and the hydrophobic segment in PEEK and the underwater lipophilicity of PEEK are the main reasons for severe membrane fouling41,42. Interestingly, the permeance of CPM remained 100% (3.4 × 104 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) even after 100 fouling-washing cycles, which was approximately 3800% greater than that of PM after fouling, indicating that the CPM did not exhibit irreversible fouling (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Figs. 43–47). This was due to the hetero-interpenetration crystal structure in the mechanical interlocking structure, which increased the rigidity of the fibers and prevented oil droplets from being embedded in the membrane due to gravity. Importantly, the rigidity of the membrane prevented it from swelling in various solvents, which greatly improved the service life of the membrane (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). In addition, the excellent antifouling performance of the prepared membrane was due to the underwater superoleophobic characteristics endowed by the introduction of COF-TpPa nanoarrays, which prevented the adhesion of oil droplets to the surface due to hydrophobic interactions. In addition, due to the formation of mechanically interlocked hydrophilic rigid COF nanoarrays, which could prevent acid/oil droplets from eroding PEEK molecular chains, the CPMs were strongly stable in various solvents and at various pH values (Supplementary Figs. 48–51), with excellent separation performance after immersion for 180 days (Fig. 4c). Interestingly, the rigid COF-TpPa nanoarray layer promoted the demulsification of the oil-in-water emulsion. The nanoscale oil-in-water emulsion enters the channel between the COF nanoarrays during the separation process. Owing to the narrow pores, the emulsion droplets continuously collided between the nanoarrays and interacted with the hydration layer, which might destroy the stability of the emulsion. Therefore, demulsification occurred inside the nanoarray, which floated on the water surface after continuous aggregation (Fig. 4d)39. In summary, the comprehensive performance of the CPMs was far greater than that of the state-of-the-art PNMs reported (Fig. 4e)43–46. Moreover, while maintaining the same retention performance, the CPM membrane achieves a permeance 59.1–90.2 μm over 8 times greater than commercial microfiltration membranes and surpasses commercial ultrafiltration membranes by two orders of magnitude (Supplementary Tables 8 and 9), showing substantial promise in oily wastewater treatment.

## Methods

Preparation of as-prepared nanofiber membranes

Preparation of PIMs. PEEKi (2.0 g) was dissolved in 8.0 g of NMP and stirred at 30 °C for 8 h to obtain a homogeneous solution. Then, a uniform PEEKi solution was poured into a disposable syringe equipped with a 0.9 mm spinneret. The applied electric voltage and solution feed rate were 13 kV and 0.0010 mm/s, respectively. The spinneret had translational oscillatory motion perpendicular to the collector rotation direction (the oscillation distance was 18 cm). A rotating collector (diameter: 10 cm, width: 20 cm) covered with glossy aluminum foil was used to collect the PEEKi nanofibers at a rotating speed of 180 rpm. The distance between the spinneret and the collector was 15 cm, and the collection time was 6 h.

Preparation of PMs. The obtained PIMs were hydrolyzed to PEEK nanofiber membranes in n-octanoic acid at 80 °C for 24 h. After that, the membranes were removed and thoroughly rinsed with deionized water. Finally, the PEEK nanofiber membranes were thermally compressed at 250 °C under 5.0 MPa for 30 min. During this procedure, the amorphous PEEK nanofiber membranes could transform into semicrystalline PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs), thereby improving the tensile strength of the nanofiber membranes.

Preparation of CPMs. Pa (1.0, 2.0 or 3.0 g) was added to the PEEKi solution to form a uniform solution. Then, uniform PEEKi-Pa solution was poured into a disposable syringe equipped with a 0.9 mm spinneret. The applied electric voltage and solution feed rate were 13 kV and 0.0010 mm/s, respectively. The spinneret had translational oscillatory motion perpendicular to the collector rotation direction (the oscillation distance was 18 cm). A rotating collector (diameter: 10 cm, width: 20 cm) covered with glossy aluminum foil was used to collect the PEEKi-Pa nanofibers at a rotating speed of 180 rpm. The distance between the spinneret and the collector was 15 cm, and the collection time was 6 h. After that, the PEEKi-Pa nanofiber membranes were soaked in Tp-n-octanoic acid solutions at 80 °C for 24 h. During this process, the Pa monomers reacted with the Tp monomers to form a COF-TpPa nanoarray layer, and PEEKi was hydrolyzed to PEEK. The as-prepared membranes were subsequently thermally compressed to obtain CPMs. The CPMs with different COF contents were labeled CPM-I, CPM-II, and CPM-III.

Full experimental procedures are available in the Supplementary Information.

crystallization process of PEEK. Sequential crystallization can effectively solve the
above problems. In this process, controlling the temperature in the process of sequential

## Paper

## Abstract

Advanced polymeric nanofiber membranes (PNMs) are hindered by intrinsically low mechanical strength and stability, especially under harsh conditions of oily water separation. Here, we report an approach to simultaneously enhance the tensile strength, stability and hydrophilicity of PNMs by sequentially crystallizing the covalent organic framework (COF) and poly(ether ether ketone) (PEEK). During the process, a superhydrophilic pine-needle-shaped COF nanoarray layer is inserted into the PEEK nanofibers to form a mechanical interlocking structure through the entanglement between PEEK non-crystallizing polymer chains and the hetero-interpenetration crystal structure consisting of COF crystal and PEEK crystal regions. Both simulation and experimental results show that the mechanical interlocking structure enhances the mechanical properties (16.2 MPa) and harsh-condition stability of the PNMs. In addition, the rigid COF nanoarray layer significantly improves the affinity with water, thereby enhancing the emulsion permeance up to 3.4 × 104 L m−2 h−1 bar−1 (968% increment) with nearly zero irreversible fouling during 100 fouling-cleaning cycles, which exceeds that of the state-of-the-art membranes.

---

## Introduction

3D printing-based electron-spinning techniques can produce nano- to micron fibers with customized characteristics, and integrated advanced polymeric nanofiber membranes (PNMs) has the characteristics of high porosity, high surface area, and adjustable structure and surface properties1–3. The superwetting nanofiber membrane developed based on the above characteristics is considered to be an indispensable tool for the oily water separation process, which rely on the different capillary force generated by the wetting properties of the membranes in water and oil4,5. However, the poor tensile strength (below 5.0 MPa) and stability of PNMs hamper their wide application because of the low crystallinity of the polymeric materials during the electrospun process, the intrinsic low strength of each nanofibers with nanoscale diameter, and low interaction between each nanofibers (Supplementary Fig. 1)6–8. Several efforts have been made to improve the tensile strength of nanofibers through inducing the force between the fibers and the regulation of the polymer crystal region7–9. The strength of nanofiber membranes can be effectively improved by inducing the formation of interaction forces, such as hydrogen bonds between fibers. However, due to its low bond energy, it is easy to destroy under extreme conditions, especially in the complex environment of water remediation9. Adjusting the crystalline region by filling the nanomaterial can also effectively improve the membrane strength, but it will destroy the stability of the non-Newtonian fluid, resulting in difficulties in the spinning process10. The development of self-supporting nanofiber membranes with high tensile strength (>15 MPa) that can be applied in various extreme environments may enhance their use in water treatment fields and promote technological change in related application fields.

Adopting the high-performance polymer as the membrane substrate can also validly facilitate the strength of the prepared membrane7. PEEK, as a typical semicrystalline polymer containing one ketone bond and two ether bonds in the main chain, has excellent high-temperature resistance, high tensile strength, good corrosion resistance and excellent stability, which is enough to cope with the extreme conditions under water environment restoration11. However, the strong solvent resistance of PEEK polymers results in extremely low solubility in various organic solvents, making membrane manufacturing a challenging process12. In addition, the inherent hydrophobicity and molecular inertness of PEEK are barriers to its application. Although the sulfonation process was used to adjust the sulfonation degree of PEEK to increase the solubility of PEEK in organic solvent, excessive sulfonation leads to poor solvent resistance in PEEK, and the corrosion of strong sulfonic acid solutions makes it difficult to modify the surface of PEEK by blending13. Moreover, the tensile strength of the membrane is still low, due to the poor molecular chain orientation during the short and weak stretching process of the non-Newtonian liquid, even if adopting the high-performance polymer, which will weaken the long-term stability in the water treatment process7. It is still a challenge to develop high-strength PEEK-based functional nanofiber membranes via mild preparation technology and modification schemes.

Herein, we conceived a facile approach to construct high-strength and stable PNMs by sequential crystallization of COF-TpPa and polyether ether ketone (PEEK). First, the Pa monomers were dissolved and uniformly distributed in a polyether ether ketone imine (PEEKi, the precursor of PEEK and transform into noncrystalline PEEK after a typical oxime hydrolysis reaction) solution and electrospun to form nanofiber membranes (PIMs-Pa). Subsequently, the crystallization process of the COF-TpPa crystal and PEEK was regulated. In this process, the existing COF crystal region will induce the crystallization process of PEEK to form a hetero-interpenetrating structure. Moreover, the amorphous polymer chains interpenetrate with each other in the crystal region to form a physically crosslinked network with a mechanical interlocking structure, thereby enhancing the strength and excellent stability (even in strong solvents, strong acid and strong base solutions) of the CPMs. Interestingly, because the dissolution of Pa and the diffusion rate are lower than the rate of COF formation, the COF crystal could grow along the radial direction of the nanofiber to form a regularly patterned COF nanoarray layer. The formation of COF nanoarrays also enhances the mechanical properties and surface hydrophilicity of CPMs and broadens their application. When deployed for the separation of an oil-in-water emulsion, owing to its intrinsic hydrophilicity and axial distribution, the regularly patterned COF-TpPa layer promoted the formation of a hydrated layer and increased the capillary force (Fig. 1a). Together with the high porosity and rigidity of the COF-TpPa, the as-prepared CPMs could provide a superhydrophilic surface, increasing the impetus and repulsion of water and defending against attack from oil droplets or oily filter cakes, thereby simultaneously improving permeances, separation efficiency and antifouling performance.

## Results

The PEEK in nanofiber membranes (PIMs), PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs), and COF-TpPa-modified PEEK nanofiber membranes (CPMs) before and after thermal compression treatment were developed (if not emphasized later, CPMs refer to CPMs-II in the Supplementary Information). The mean diameter of the PMs was approximately 0.16 ± 0.1 μm (Supplementary Figs. 3–5), and no obvious adhesion between individual nanofibers was observed. Due to the increase of the viscosity of the casting solution, the diameter of PIMs-Pa increased to 1.02 μm, which may significantly influence the characteristics of the prepared membrane (Supplementary Table 1). For the CPMs, axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF nanoarrays uniformly appeared on the surface of the nanofibers, and the diameter and length of the pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray were 45.4 and 151.6 nm, respectively (Fig. 1e, f). The diameter of the CPMs (approximately 1.44 μm) was approximately equal to the sum of the diameter of the pure PIM-Pa membrane (1.02 μm) and the thickness of the nanoarrays, indicating that the growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer greatly increased the diameter of the fibers (Fig. 1b, c and Supplementary Fig. 5). Notably, the morphology of the PMs and CPMs after thermal compression treatment was identical to that of the PMs and CPMs without thermal compression treatment (Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating that the as-prepared nanofibers could maintain shape stability even under a pressure of 5.0 MPa during the thermal treatment. In addition, the thickness of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes increased from 59.1 to 90.2 μm after the in situ growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray due to the uncompacted stacking of thicker fibers, which may also reduce the mass transfer resistance during the separation process (Supplementary Fig. 7)4. Moreover, the growth of nanoarrays greatly improves the specific surface area of the prepared membrane, expanding the steric hindrance between the oil molecules and membrane surface (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Interestingly, the in situ growth of the COF nanoarray layer regulates the crystallinity of PEEK molecules, and transmission electron microscopy confirmed the formation of interpenetrated structures between crystal regions (Fig. 1g)14,15. Before thermal compression, the PMs were amorphous, while one type of lattice fringe with the 0.22 nm d-spacing was observed for the PMs after thermal treatment (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). The lattice fringe of COF-TpPa with d-spacing of 0.3 nm appeared on the CPMs before thermal compression (Supplementary Fig. 9c)16. Notably, the introduction of COFs led to the disappearance of most of the lattice fringes of the PMs, and the electron diffraction pattern demonstrated the transformation from a single crystal to polycrystalline with a variety of lattice fringes with different d-spacings after thermal treatment (Fig. 1g and Supplementary Fig. 9c). Furthermore, d-spacings within the crystalline domains of PEEK and COF-TpPa exhibited a marginal increase, attributable to lattice distortion arising from the thermally induced slip of COF crystals by PEEK16,17. Moreover, the surface roughness of the nanofiber membranes increased by 30%-85% after the formation of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer (Supplementary Fig. 10), which could affect the surface energy of the membrane18,19. Interestingly, the membrane aperture and membrane porosity increased by 105% and 102%, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 11 and 12), because the COF-TpPa nanoarray increased the distance between the nanofibers.

According to density functional theory, the Gibbs free energy of molecules in different reaction stages was calculated to clarify the limit of the thermodynamic direction of the chemical reaction process20. The energy barrier of p-phenylenediamine bound to PEEKi is 72.3 kcal/mol, which is less than that bound to aniline. Therefore, p-phenylenediamine alleviated the hydrolysis process of PEEKi oxime (Fig. 1h)18. Interestingly, aniline, the byproduct of oxime hydrolysis, would not exert significant negative feedback on the formation process of COF-TpPa due to the large Gibbs free energy of reaction between aniline and Tp (Supplementary Fig. 13)21. On the basis of the above experimental and simulation results, the mechanism of the formation of the unique microstructure of the CPMs was speculated. As mentioned above, the hydrolysis of PEEKi and in situ growth of COF-TpPa simultaneously occurred in n-octanoic acid solutions. Since the solubility and diffusion rate of Pa in n-octanoic acid were far lower than the rate of COF-TpPa formation, especially the -CHO of Tp, which was activated to -C+HOH by n-octanoic acid in the solvent (Supplementary Fig. 14)22, the in situ growth of the COF-TpPa layer mainly occurred at the interface between the nanofibers and n-octanoic acid. With the continuous diffusion and dissolution of an appropriate content of Pa, the formation of an axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray on the top surface of PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs) was induced and inserted (Fig. 2a). Notably, as the Pa content increased, the COF-TpPa layer formed distinct nanostructures, including nanobulges, pine-needle-shaped nanoarrays, and nanoflowers (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). This morphological evolution was driven by the number of surface Pa reactive sites and the enhanced diffusion rate (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 15). After the formation of the COF-TpPa nanoarray, the hydrolysis of PEEKi became easier without the inhibition caused by Pa. Simultaneously, the hydrolysis of PEEKi released aniline, which reduced the steric hindrance of the subsequent thermal rearrangement crystallization process so that the thermal rearrangement of the polymer chain was easier to carry out (Fig. 2b).

This sequential crystallization could optimize the compatibility between COF and PEEK crystals and avoid phase separation. Therefore, the molecules of crystalline PEEK and COF-TpPa formed a hetero-interpenetration crystal structure, and the noncrystalline PEEK molecules wrapped the interpenetrating crystals to form mechanically interlocked structures23–25. The changes in the chemical structure and properties of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes further confirmed the above speculation (Supplementary Figs. 16–19 and Supplementary Table 2), which are discussed in detail in the Supplementary Infomation11,26,27. The sequential crystallization of COF-TpPa and PEEK could be confirmed by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 20). PEEKi and PEEK were fully amorphous after electron pinning, with no characteristic diffraction peaks. Notably, only the COF-TpPa crystal pattern (2θ = 4.6°) appeared in the XRD pattern of the CPMs before thermal treatment. The crystallinity of COF-TpPa was approximately 13.0%. After thermal compression treatment, new characteristic peaks belonging to the PEEK crystal region (2θ = 18.2°) in the PMs and CPMs were observed28. In addition, the XRD characteristic diffraction peaks of both COF-TpPa and PEEK shifted to the left, which also confirmed the increase in d-spacing caused by the interpenetration between the COF crystal and the PEEK crystal23,27–30. The crystallinity (41.4%) of PEEK in CPMs was slightly lower than that in PMs (43.3%) since COF-TpPa restricted the rearrangement of the molecular chain of PEEK, thereby limiting their crystallization (Supplementary Table 3)29–31. The melting temperature of PMs was approximately 250 °C, but the CPMs did not melt even at 400 °C (Supplementary Fig. 21). Moreover, the (Tg) of the CPMs increased by 15.1 °C after the introduction of the COF-TpPa layer and the sequential crystallization of the COF and PEEK (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 22)32. Molecular dynamics (MD) calculations show that compared with the original PEEK, the free volume of PEEK containing COF-TpPa is reduced by 37.8%, indicating that the introduction of COF-TpPa limits the movement of the PEEK main chain and causes a decrease in crystallinity, as mentioned above (Supplementary Fig. 23). Consequently, the glass transition temperature of CPMs is higher than that of PMs. The tensile strength of the PIM was approximately 2.3 MPa (Fig. 2e). The rigid structure of PEEK contributes to its high tensile strength. Interestingly, the crystallization process of PEEK increased its tensile strength by 121.7%. The strength of the CPMs after sequential crystallization increased to 16.2 MPa, which was comparable with that of laboratory-made ultrafiltration membranes fabricated by nonsolvent-induced phase inversion (Supplementary Fig. 24). Notably, the increase in tensile strength was positively correlated with the content of the COF-TpPa (Supplementary Table 4), which showed that the introduction of a COF had a great influence on the mechanical properties of PEEK. As mentioned above, COF-TpPa is a crystalline material composed of conjugated aromatic rings, showing strong intrinsic rigidity11. Moreover, the molecular rearrangement transforms randomly because the thermal compression arranges the molecular chain segments of PEEK into long-range ordered arrangements. The hetero-interpenetration crystal structure formed by COF-TpPa and crystalline PEEK molecules contributed to the increase in the tensile strength of each nanofiber33. Interestingly, the introduction of COF led to an increase in the proportion of the amorphous region, which could absorb energy through slip and conformational changes in the molecular chain when subjected to external force, thereby increasing the elongation at break of the nanofiber membrane (Fig. 2f)34,35. The mechanical interlocking structure formed by amorphous molecules and hetero-interpenetration crystal structures optimistically increases the mechanical properties of nanofiber membranes. In addition, the nanofiber membranes were stacked by every single nanofiber of the CPMs, as mentioned above. The stacking of the axially distributed pine-needle-shaped COF-TpPa nanoarray improved the interactive force (friction force) between different nanofibers, which could increase the mechanical strength of the prepared membrane by dispersing the force between the fibers through friction (Fig. 2f). Significantly, compared with PMs, CPMs have unparalleled stability in most organic solvents. The CPMs still maintained the shape of intact fibers after soaking in various organic solvents for 180 days, but the fibers of the PMs partially collapsed, which may have been caused by incomplete hydrolysis (Supplementary Fig. 25). Interestingly, the COF nanoarrays collapsed in some solvents, resulting in a slight decrease in tensile strength, which also proved that pine-needle-like nanoarrays between different fibers could enhance the tensile properties of the prepared membranes by dispersing external forces via friction. Notably, the prepared CPMs still had high tensile strength and elongation at break (Fig. 2g).

Interestingly, the COF-TpPa nanoarray excellently increased the surface energy of the PMs. The PMs demonstrated high hydrophobicity and underwater superoleophilicity, with a stable water contact angle of approximately 135.1° and a zero degree of underwater oil contact angle (UWOCA). However, water droplets could spread on the surface of the CPMs in less than 1.0 s, and the UWOCA of the CPM membranes was above 150.3°, indicating that the hydrophobic surface of the PM had transformed into a superhydrophilic surface after in situ radical growth of the COF-TpPa nanoarray (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Movies 1, 2 and Fig. 26). The underwater oil rolling angle of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes decreased to 5.4° after the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarrays (Supplementary Figs. 27, 28 and Supplementary Movie 3). In addition, unlike the superoleophilic PMs, the CPMs exhibited excellent oil repellency, and the adhesion force of the underwater oil droplets was less than 1.0 μN (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Movie 4 and Supplementary Fig. 29). The increase (51.8 times) in the apparent surface tension of the polar components caused by the abundant conjugated oxygen-containing groups in COF-TpPa and increased surface roughness (58.5%) on the nanofiber surface account for the reversal of surface hydrophilicity (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 30)36.

As a kind of hydrophobic material, the water adsorption capacity of PM is as low as 0.8 g g−1. After the formation of the COF-TpPa crystal nanoarray layer, the water adsorption capacity was nearly 14.8 times greater than that of the PMs since the CPMs contained many water adsorption sites and conjugated oxygen-containing groups (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 31)37. Moreover, the endothermic peak of the water-melting process shifted from 0.29 to 4.26 °C with more melting enthalpy (156.49 J/g) after the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarray. Similarly, the content of nonrefrigerated water in the CPMs (37.7%) was much greater than that in the PMs (18.4%) (Fig. 3e). In addition, the peak area ratios of intermediate water (3216 and 3400 cm−1) and free water (3544 and 3700 cm−1) increased from 0.21 to 1.75 according to Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3f; Supplementary Fig. 32 and Supplementary Table 5), which further proved that the water binding capacity of the as-prepared nanofiber membranes significantly increased as well38. According to the MD simulation, the CPM membranes exhibited stronger electrostatic interactions with water (Ecoul), which could induce a stronger binding ability with water (Fig. 3g, h)39. The water molecular diffusion coefficients in the hydration layers of the PM and CPMs were 2.6 and 2.0 m2/s, respectively. Moreover, the residence time of the CPM hydration layer was also greater than that of the PM hydration layer. The lower diffusion coefficient and greater water residence time in the CPMs could also account for their greater ability to form a hydration layer (Supplementary Fig. 33)40. In addition, the ability to form hydrogen bonds between water and the PNMs and the lifetime of the hydrogen bonds increased by 62.5% and 58.6%, respectively, after the introduction of COF-TpPa nanoarrays (Fig. 3j and Supplementary Fig. 34), which was attributed to the formation of hydrophilic COF nanoarrays on the fiber providing a large number of potential hydrogen bond acceptor sites and donor sites. (Supplementary Fig. 35)37.

The superhydrophilic surface of the engineered membrane significantly expands its potential applications in diverse operational environments, such as oil-water separation. Owing to the intrinsically hydrophobic surface, the pristine PM had a low permeance of 3.2 × 103 L m−2 h−1 bar−1, with a separation efficiency of 92.7% for water-in-octane emulsions. The permeance of the CPMs increased significantly by at least 968% and was positively correlated with the content of COF-TpPa (Fig. 4a; Supplementary Figs. 36 and 37), and the separation efficiency of the CPMs was above 99.9% (Fig. 4a). The increased permeance and separation efficiency after in situ radical growth of the COF-TpPa crystal layer could be attributed to the finely tailored membrane structures and affinities with water during the dynamic crystal engineering process, according to both the experimental and simulation results mentioned above. The COF-TpPa nanoarray layer increased the mean pore size of the nanofiber membranes, reducing the mass transfer resistance (Supplementary Fig. 38). The improvement in the affinity between the nanofiber membranes and water caused by the introduction of the COF-TpPa nanoarray layer during the sequential crystallization process promoted the formation of a rigid hydration layer and encouraged water to pass through the nanofiber membranes while preventing the formation of oil droplets (Fig. 4d). More importantly, the mean particle size of the oil droplets in the filtrate of CPM was less than 100 nm, which was far smaller than that in the feed emulsion (1000 nm) and in the filtrate of PMs (500 nm) (Supplementary Fig. 38). Notably, the average pore diameter of the CPMs was greater than 3 μm, indicating that the separation of the oil-water emulsions was dependent mainly on the different Laplace repulsions caused by the different wettabilities toward water and oil2,39,40. The CPMs were also effective at disposing of various oil-in-water emulsions, such as toluene-in-water emulsions and soybean-in-water emulsions (Supplementary Figs. 39–41).

During the separation process of nanofiber membranes, the oil droplets tend to adhere and embed into the nanofiber membranes via hydrophobic interactions under transmembrane pressure due to the flexible segment and hydrophobicity of the polymer, resulting in severe irreversible membrane fouling, which limits the application of nanofiber membranes in oil/water separation (Supplementary Fig. 42). The PM exhibited severe irreversible fouling since the permeance decreased to 7.0 × 102 L m−2 h−1 bar−1, and the separation efficiency correspondingly decreased to 80% after 100 fouling-washing cycles. The interaction between the oily cake layer and the hydrophobic segment in PEEK and the underwater lipophilicity of PEEK are the main reasons for severe membrane fouling41,42. Interestingly, the permeance of CPM remained 100% (3.4 × 104 L m−2 h−1 bar−1) even after 100 fouling-washing cycles, which was approximately 3800% greater than that of PM after fouling, indicating that the CPM did not exhibit irreversible fouling (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Figs. 43–47). This was due to the hetero-interpenetration crystal structure in the mechanical interlocking structure, which increased the rigidity of the fibers and prevented oil droplets from being embedded in the membrane due to gravity. Importantly, the rigidity of the membrane prevented it from swelling in various solvents, which greatly improved the service life of the membrane (Supplementary Tables 6 and 7). In addition, the excellent antifouling performance of the prepared membrane was due to the underwater superoleophobic characteristics endowed by the introduction of COF-TpPa nanoarrays, which prevented the adhesion of oil droplets to the surface due to hydrophobic interactions. In addition, due to the formation of mechanically interlocked hydrophilic rigid COF nanoarrays, which could prevent acid/oil droplets from eroding PEEK molecular chains, the CPMs were strongly stable in various solvents and at various pH values (Supplementary Figs. 48–51), with excellent separation performance after immersion for 180 days (Fig. 4c). Interestingly, the rigid COF-TpPa nanoarray layer promoted the demulsification of the oil-in-water emulsion. The nanoscale oil-in-water emulsion enters the channel between the COF nanoarrays during the separation process. Owing to the narrow pores, the emulsion droplets continuously collided between the nanoarrays and interacted with the hydration layer, which might destroy the stability of the emulsion. Therefore, demulsification occurred inside the nanoarray, which floated on the water surface after continuous aggregation (Fig. 4d)39. In summary, the comprehensive performance of the CPMs was far greater than that of the state-of-the-art PNMs reported (Fig. 4e)43–46. Moreover, while maintaining the same retention performance, the CPM membrane achieves a permeance 59.1–90.2 μm over 8 times greater than commercial microfiltration membranes and surpasses commercial ultrafiltration membranes by two orders of magnitude (Supplementary Tables 8 and 9), showing substantial promise in oily wastewater treatment.

## Methods

Preparation of as-prepared nanofiber membranes

Preparation of PIMs. PEEKi (2.0 g) was dissolved in 8.0 g of NMP and stirred at 30 °C for 8 h to obtain a homogeneous solution. Then, a uniform PEEKi solution was poured into a disposable syringe equipped with a 0.9 mm spinneret. The applied electric voltage and solution feed rate were 13 kV and 0.0010 mm/s, respectively. The spinneret had translational oscillatory motion perpendicular to the collector rotation direction (the oscillation distance was 18 cm). A rotating collector (diameter: 10 cm, width: 20 cm) covered with glossy aluminum foil was used to collect the PEEKi nanofibers at a rotating speed of 180 rpm. The distance between the spinneret and the collector was 15 cm, and the collection time was 6 h.

Preparation of PMs. The obtained PIMs were hydrolyzed to PEEK nanofiber membranes in n-octanoic acid at 80 °C for 24 h. After that, the membranes were removed and thoroughly rinsed with deionized water. Finally, the PEEK nanofiber membranes were thermally compressed at 250 °C under 5.0 MPa for 30 min. During this procedure, the amorphous PEEK nanofiber membranes could transform into semicrystalline PEEK nanofiber membranes (PMs), thereby improving the tensile strength of the nanofiber membranes.

Preparation of CPMs. Pa (1.0, 2.0 or 3.0 g) was added to the PEEKi solution to form a uniform solution. Then, uniform PEEKi-Pa solution was poured into a disposable syringe equipped with a 0.9 mm spinneret. The applied electric voltage and solution feed rate were 13 kV and 0.0010 mm/s, respectively. The spinneret had translational oscillatory motion perpendicular to the collector rotation direction (the oscillation distance was 18 cm). A rotating collector (diameter: 10 cm, width: 20 cm) covered with glossy aluminum foil was used to collect the PEEKi-Pa nanofibers at a rotating speed of 180 rpm. The distance between the spinneret and the collector was 15 cm, and the collection time was 6 h. After that, the PEEKi-Pa nanofiber membranes were soaked in Tp-n-octanoic acid solutions at 80 °C for 24 h. During this process, the Pa monomers reacted with the Tp monomers to form a COF-TpPa nanoarray layer, and PEEKi was hydrolyzed to PEEK. The as-prepared membranes were subsequently thermally compressed to obtain CPMs. The CPMs with different COF contents were labeled CPM-I, CPM-II, and CPM-III.

Full experimental procedures are available in the Supplementary Information.

crystals form lattice interpenetrating structures, which greatly improved the mechanical

the membrane was improved by the slip of the molecules in the amorphous region to

provide a large number of potential hydrogen bond acceptor sites and donor sites. By
virtue of its strong polarity and bifunctional (donor and acceptor) properties, water
molecules can form hydrogen bond networks with these sites very effectively (Small,

high specific surface area and pore structure of the COF material, water molecules can
fully contact these sites, resulting in a significant hydrogen bond interaction between
COF-TpPa and water (Fig. R5). According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have
revised and supplemented the relevant mechanism diagram in order to expect readers
to understand our point of view.

1. After in-situ growth of COF-TpPa nanoarrays, the thickness of the nanofiber
membrane increased from 59.1 μm to 90.2 μm. What is the reason for the increase in
thickness, and will it affect the mass transfer process of the membrane?
Responses: Thanks for your insightful comments. The increase of membrane thickness
was mainly due to the formation of nanoarrays. The diameter was further increased by
about 0.42 μm after the formation of in-situ nanoarrays (Fig. 3d), which caused the
spacing between the fibers to widen. The increase in thickness means that the fiber stack
is not dense and the porosity increases, which will lead to a decrease in the mass transfer
resistance of the permeate during the separation process and improve the permeance of
the prepared membrane. (ACS Nano, 2022, 16, 4684-4692). Meanwhile, due to the
growth of surface COF nanoarrays, the hydrophilicity of the membrane surface is
improved, so the separation efficiency is also greatly improved.

4. It can be seen from the XRD spectrum that the crystallinity of COF decreased after
hot pressing. Will this cause a decrease in membrane performance.
Responses: We appreciated your mentioned about this point. The weakening
crystallinity of COF is mainly due to the slip of the COF crystal during the thermal
motion of PEEK. We compared the separation performance of CPM before and after
crystallization, and the results were not much different. Notably, the mechanical
properties of PEEK improved significantly after crystallization. The separation process
of the membrane to the emulsion mainly depends on the surface morphology and
surface wettability of the membrane. The change of COF crystallinity did not affect the
apparent morphology and contact angle (Fig. R10b and Fig. R11), so the decrease of
COF crystallinity had little effect on the separation performance of the membrane (Fig.
R10a).

6. Whether the author can supplement BET and other characterizations to improve the
basic properties of nanofiber membranes after in-situ growth of COF to build solid
structural advantages.
Responses: We appreciate your suggestion. We supplemented the BET adsorption curve
and specific surface area test of CPMs and PMs. The results showed that the adsorption
isotherm of CPMs belonged to type IV isotherm, and there was a significant increase
in the amount of adsorption in the high relative pressure area. The CPMs on the surface
had a certain porous structure. The adsorption capacity of PMs was almost zero,
indicating that fibers of PMs had almost no pore structure. Moreover, the specific
surface area of CPMs was significantly higher than that of PMs, which was due to the
contribution of CPM surface nanoarrays. The larger specific surface area increased the
contact interface between the membrane and water, expanding the steric hindrance
between the oil molecules and membrane surface (Nat. Commun. 2015, 14, 2679).
